clarity.justification: The method directly targets the hypothesis through the directional predictions that “convergent same-mechanism enzymes will cluster in a mechanism subspace despite low sequence identity, while divergent homologs will separate” and that catalytic-residue ablation will degrade decoding “more than ablating matched non-catalytic residues.” These measurements could refute the claim if the predicted clustering/separation is absent or if catalytic-position ablation performs no differently from the control, but no numeric decision threshold is supplied. Important details remain ambiguous, including the operational definition of “mechanism classes,” the exact construction of the “mechanism-vs-homology discriminability index,” and whether “attention or high-attribution features” is the decisive residue-grounding metric.

feasibility.justification: The named dependencies—“M-CSA,” “Swiss-Prot,” and “ESM-2”—exist, and standard protein-model inference, probing, attribution, clustering, regression, and token-level intervention tooling supports most of the proposed operations. The hardest step is assembling defensible sets of “non-homologous same-mechanism enzymes” and “homologous different-mechanism enzymes” while “controlling for % sequence identity”; this is custom dataset and analysis engineering rather than a magic step, although the grouping and regression procedures are not specified. The matched-residue ablation control and the convergence/divergence comparison make the refuting branch runnable, despite the acknowledged possibility that “a negative result may reflect probe weakness.” Resources are only broadly named—there are no sample counts, identity cutoffs, ESM-2 sizes, layer choices, or other concrete scale figures—so an implementer must make several consequential design decisions before starting.
